title: Which design pattern is used for synchronous communication between microservices (API Gateway)?
shortTitle: Design pattern for synchronous communication between microservices

s1_definition.profdef: The primary design pattern for synchronous communication between microservices and their clients is the API Gateway pattern, which places a single entry point in front of the services to handle routing, authentication, rate limiting, request aggregation, and protocol translation, so clients make one synchronous call instead of many direct calls to individual services. It is commonly paired with supporting synchronous patterns: Service Discovery so the gateway and services resolve each other by logical name, client-side Load Balancing to spread calls across healthy instances, and the Circuit Breaker to fail fast when a downstream synchronous call is unhealthy. A related variant is Backend-for-Frontend, where a dedicated gateway is tailored to each client type.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, the API Gateway is the single reception desk at the front of the bank. Instead of Rajesh running from the accounts counter to the payments counter to the cards counter himself, he hands one request to reception, which checks his ID once, limits how many requests flood in per minute, and then goes to the right counters on his behalf and brings back a combined answer. Reception also knows which counter is open today (service discovery) and sends him to whichever teller is free (load balancing), and if a counter is closed it tells him quickly instead of making him wait forever (circuit breaker).
s1_definition.oneliner: The API Gateway pattern is the single synchronous entry point that routes, authenticates, rate-limits, and aggregates calls to services, supported by service discovery, load balancing, and circuit breakers.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The primary design pattern for synchronous communication between microservices and their clients is the API Gateway pattern, which places a single entry point in front of the services to handle routing, authentication, rate limiting, request aggregation, and protocol translation, so clients make one synchronous call instead of many direct calls to individual services. It is commonly paired with supporting synchronous patterns: Service Discovery so the gateway and services resolve each other by logical name, client-side Load Balancing to spread calls across healthy instances, and the Circuit Breaker to fail fast when a downstream synchronous call is unhealthy. A related variant is Backend-for-Frontend, where a dedicated gateway is tailored to each client type.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, the API Gateway is the single reception desk at the front of the bank. Instead of Rajesh running from the accounts counter to the payments counter to the cards counter himself, he hands one request to reception, which checks his ID once, limits how many requests flood in per minute, and then goes to the right counters on his behalf and brings back a combined answer. Reception also knows which counter is open today (service discovery) and sends him to whichever teller is free (load balancing), and if a counter is closed it tells him quickly instead of making him wait forever (circuit breaker).

**One line to remember:** The API Gateway pattern is the single synchronous entry point that routes, authenticates, rate-limits, and aggregates calls to services, supported by service discovery, load balancing, and circuit breakers.

sections.s2_technical:
The API Gateway pattern centralizes everything a client should not have to do itself. A route is a predicate plus filters: in Spring Cloud Gateway you route `Path=/api/v1/payments/**` to `lb://payment-service` and attach filters for JWT authentication and a `RequestRateLimiter`. Because the gateway is the single front door, you enforce cross-cutting concerns once rather than copying them into every service, and you hide the internal topology so services can be split or renamed without changing clients.

Request aggregation is a core benefit for synchronous flows. A mobile dashboard needs account, payment, and card data, and without a gateway the app would make three synchronous round trips and know three internal addresses. With the gateway, the app makes one synchronous call to `/api/v1/dashboard`, and the gateway fans out to the three services, waits for all responses, and merges them. This reduces client complexity and network chatter, and it is where the Backend-for-Frontend variant helps: a separate gateway per client type, so the mobile gateway returns a lean payload while the web gateway returns a richer one.

The gateway relies on supporting synchronous patterns. Service Discovery means the gateway resolves `lb://payment-service` through a registry like Eureka to a live instance rather than a hardcoded address, which matters because instances scale up and down. Client-side Load Balancing spreads calls across healthy instances, so no single instance is overloaded. The Circuit Breaker wraps each downstream synchronous call, for example a `CircuitBreaker` filter with a `fallbackUri`, so when the payment service is unhealthy the gateway fails fast and returns a fallback instead of hanging and exhausting its own threads.

Protocol translation is another gateway job: the public edge speaks REST and JSON over HTTP/1.1, while internal calls may be gRPC over HTTP/2, and the gateway translates between them so clients stay simple. The senior-level nuance is that the gateway must not become a monolith of business logic; it handles routing, security, aggregation, and resilience, but the actual business rules live in the services. Overloading the gateway with domain logic recreates the very coupling microservices were meant to remove, so a disciplined gateway stays thin and generic while the services stay authoritative.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the mobile app shows Rajesh a dashboard. Problem 1 — without a gateway the app makes three synchronous calls to the account, payment, and card services, embedding internal addresses and repeating authentication in each call. This is exactly what the API Gateway pattern solves with one authenticated, aggregated call. Problem 2 — the payment service runs several instances that scale with load, so the gateway cannot hardcode an address. This is exactly what service discovery plus load balancing solve. Problem 3 — the card service goes slow, and the gateway must not hang waiting for it. This is exactly what the circuit breaker solves by failing fast with a fallback.

The mini-project models an `ApiGateway` that authenticates once, discovers and load-balances instances, aggregates three service calls synchronously, and wraps each in a circuit breaker. A runnable demo serves a dashboard request, shows traffic choosing a healthy instance, and shows the card service failing with the gateway returning a graceful fallback.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a dashboard request for Rajesh (SAV2001) with a valid JWT, then the same request while the card service is down.

Step 1: The mobile app makes one synchronous call to the gateway. The gateway checks the JWT once. If it were missing the request would be rejected with a security error; here it is valid, so the request proceeds. Authentication happens in exactly one place.

Step 2: The gateway begins aggregation. For the account service it asks the registry to choose a healthy instance, performs service discovery and load balancing, then makes a synchronous call and receives the account data.

Step 3: The gateway repeats for the payment service, again discovering an instance and calling it synchronously. Each call is wrapped so a failure in one does not abort the whole dashboard.

Step 4: The gateway calls the card service. In the healthy run it succeeds, and the gateway merges account, payment, and card data into one response for the client, which made only a single round trip.

Step 5: Now the card service is down. The gateway's call to it throws, and the circuit-breaker-style handler fails fast and substitutes a `card-service-UNAVAILABLE` fallback instead of hanging. The dashboard still returns account and payment data, so one failing downstream does not take down the whole screen.

```text
Oct 24, 2026 11:54:20 INFO === Single synchronous call → gateway aggregates three services ===
Oct 24, 2026 11:54:20 INFO Gateway authenticated + aggregating for SAV2001
Oct 24, 2026 11:54:20 INFO SYNC call to account-service for SAV2001
Oct 24, 2026 11:54:20 INFO SYNC call to payment-service for SAV2001
Oct 24, 2026 11:54:20 INFO SYNC call to card-service for SAV2001
Oct 24, 2026 11:54:20 INFO Dashboard: {account=account-service-data, payment=payment-service-data, card=card-service-data}
Oct 24, 2026 11:54:20 INFO === Card service down → gateway fails fast with fallback ===

Oct 24, 2026 11:54:20 INFO SYNC call to payment-service for SAV2001

```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Mobile App: GET /api/v1/dashboard?accountId=SAV2001 (JWT)
    │ ONE synchronous call
    ▼
  API Gateway
    │ authenticate JWT ✓ (once)
    │ rate limit ✓
    │ aggregate (fan-out, wait for all) ─ each call: discover → load-balance → breaker
    ├──→ account-service (SYNC) → account-data
    ├──→ payment-service (SYNC) → payment-data
    └──→ card-service    (SYNC) → card-data
                                   │ if DOWN → fail fast → card-UNAVAILABLE
    ▼
  merge → {account, payment, card}
    ▼
  ONE response to the app (not three round trips)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — API Gateway Pattern ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ API Gateway: single entry point, route+auth+aggregate.    │
  │   WHY: one synchronous call, hide topology, centralize.  │
  │ Service Discovery + Load Balancing: ServiceRegistry.      │
  │   WHY: resolve logical names, spread across instances.  │
  │ Circuit Breaker: callWithBreaker fails fast on failure.   │
  │ Backend-for-Frontend: a gateway tailored per client type. │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: gateway routes/aggregates, registry discovers,         │
  │    services own business logic (thin gateway).            │
  │ O: new backend = register it + add a call, no rewrite.    │
  │ D: gateway depends on ServiceRegistry abstraction.        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌────────────────────┐   uses   ┌─────────────────────┐
  │    ApiGateway      │─────────►│  ServiceRegistry    │
  │ - registry         │          │ - instances: Map    │
  │ + dashboard(jwt,id)│          │ + register(name,i)  │
  │ - callWithBreaker()│          │ + choose(name)      │ (round-robin LB)
  └─────────┬──────────┘          └──────────┬──────────┘
            │ calls *                          │ holds *
            ▼                                  ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                 BackendService                       │
  │ - name ; - down                                      │
  │ + fetch(accountId): String   (throws ServiceException)│
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: A Downstream Call ───────────────────────

  [CALL] ──instance healthy──→ [SUCCESS → data]
     │ instance throws
     ▼
  [FAIL FAST] ──→ [FALLBACK returned] (dashboard still renders rest)

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. ApiGateway.dashboard("valid-jwt","SAV2001")
  2.   → verify JWT ✓ (auth once)
  3.   → callWithBreaker("account-service","SAV2001")
  4.       → registry.choose(...) → instance → fetch() → data
  5.   → callWithBreaker("payment-service","SAV2001") → data
  6.   → callWithBreaker("card-service","SAV2001")
  7.       → down? → fail fast → "card-service-UNAVAILABLE"
  8.   → merge → one response
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The primary design pattern for synchronous communication between microservices and their clients is the API Gateway pattern. It places a single entry point in front of all the services, so instead of a client making many direct synchronous calls and knowing every internal address, it makes one call to the gateway. In my banking work at National Bank of India, the mobile app requests Rajesh's dashboard with a single authenticated call, and the gateway handles routing, authentication, rate limiting, request aggregation, and protocol translation on its behalf.

Request aggregation is the part that matters most for synchronous flows. The dashboard needs account, payment, and card data, and without a gateway the app would make three round trips and embed three internal addresses. With the gateway, the app makes one call, the gateway fans out to the three services synchronously, waits for all of them, and merges the responses into one payload. When I need different shapes for different clients, I use the Backend-for-Frontend variant, with a lean gateway for mobile and a richer one for web.

The gateway never works alone; it relies on supporting synchronous patterns. Service Discovery, usually Eureka, lets the gateway resolve a logical name like payment-service to a live instance rather than a hardcoded address, which matters because instances scale up and down. Client-side Load Balancing spreads calls across healthy instances. The Circuit Breaker wraps each downstream call, so when the card service went down in my example, the gateway failed fast and returned a graceful fallback instead of hanging, and the dashboard still rendered the account and payment data.

The discipline I always stress is that the gateway must stay thin. It handles routing, security, aggregation, and resilience, but the actual business rules live in the services. If you start pushing domain logic into the gateway, it becomes a new monolith and recreates exactly the coupling that microservices were meant to remove. So a healthy API Gateway is generic and authoritative about cross-cutting concerns, while the services remain authoritative about the business.
